item.content:encoded:
Architecture studio Kuryłowicz + Architects has revealed photos of the timber Arctowski Station nearing completion on King George Island in Antarctica.

Currently under construction, the three-pronged research station has a prefabricated timber structure clad in insulated golden panels.

Kuryłowicz + Architects designed the base to be a home away from home for the 28 researchers working at the Polish research station.

"The main idea was to create a 'home at the end of the world': a place that combines scientific functionality with the comfort of everyday living," said Kuryłowicz + Architects architect Piotr Kuczynski.

"The station is not just a laboratory, but a temporary home for people working in one of the most extreme environments on Earth," he continued.

"A central shared space, natural materials, and areas designed for social interaction support not only research activities but also the well-being of the residents. It is a warm Polish home protected by an intelligent outer shell, enabling people to live and work in harmony with Antarctica."

At the centre of the Arctowski Station will be a communal hub, housed in a double-height, top-lit space. It will also contain a library, gym and sauna.

According to the studio, this focus on comfort differentiates it from the majority of Antarctic research bases.

"What distinguishes the project is its ambition to bring human emotion and beauty to a place where they are least expected," said Kuryłowicz + Architects.

"Through the use of natural materials, carefully crafted interior spaces, and a strong visual connection to the surrounding landscape, the station becomes more than a piece of infrastructure," it continued. "It offers a sense of comfort, inspiration, and belonging, transforming a remote scientific outpost into a meaningful place to live and work."

The research centre was constructed from mass-timber elements that were supported on steel stilts to raise the base off the ground. It was then wrapped in a golden-coloured metal skin with extensive insulation.

This entire structure was designed to be shipped to Antarctica in 113 shipping containers and assembled within a three-month-long building window.

Read:

Eight Antarctic buildings that "have the X Factor"

"Modularity was the foundation of the entire architectural concept," said Kuczynski. "Every component had to fit inside a shipping container, survive sea transport, and be assembled quickly during the short Antarctic summer."

"These transportation constraints shaped the building's form, but they also influenced its character," he continued. "The interior, made from wood sourced from Polish forests, provides warmth and comfort while symbolically recalling the spirit of the first explorers, who carried a piece of home with them on their journeys."

"The building's metal 'skin', in contrast, represents contemporary technological achievements. Together, they create a fusion of nostalgia and 'newstalgia' – a dialogue between history and the future," he added.

Arctowski Station is the latest in Antarctica designed to withstand some of the harshest environmental conditions on Earth. These conditions largely determined the building's three-pronged form.

"Antarctica was the most important design factor," said Kuczynski. "The building had to withstand winds of up to 160 kilometre per hour, temperatures below -20° Calcius, snow, sea salt, and challenging ground conditions."

"Its three-winged form ensures access to sunlight in the most important areas, reduces snow accumulation, and elevates the building approximately three meters above the ground, allowing wind to flow freely beneath and over it, much like around an aircraft wing," he continued.

Other research bases in Antarctica recently featured on Dezeen include the Antarctic Discovery Building by Hugh Broughton Architects and NORR and a prefabricated station for Brazil by Estúdio 41.

item.content:encoded:
British architecture studio Foster + Partners has been cleared over the death of a man killed by a window that fell from one of its buildings in London, following a five-week criminal trial.

The case concerned the Corniche, a tower block of luxury flats standing close to the south side of the Thames on Albert Embankment, as part of a development that completed in 2019.

Mick Ferris, a 53-year-old coach driver, was killed instantly on 2 October 2018 when he was struck by a 130-kilogram window that had fallen 90 metres from the penthouse of the building down to the street below.

The outward-opening window had been blown off its hinges with the building close to completion, the court heard. A metal restrictor to prevent that from happening had been removed.

After more than 11 hours of deliberation at Inner London Crown Court, the jury concluded that neither Foster + Partners nor the building's design engineer, engineering consultancy Wintech, should be held responsible for the death, the Guardian reported.

But the building's project manager, property developer St James Group, and project engineer, contractor Lindner Prater, were both found guilty of failing in their duty to keep the public safe under the Health and Safety at Work Act 1974. All four defendants had denied the charges.

"An accident waiting to happen again"

The prosecution was brought by government agency the Health and Safety Executive, which had claimed the designers had ignored concerns about the proven danger posed by outward-opening, side-hung windows.

It had argued that Foster + Partners should have been aware of such risks given that glass-covered buildings are "something of a speciality" for the firm.

The designers were accused of failing to consider the "catastrophic" consequences of something going wrong with the restrictor, and of failing to take into account the fulcrum effect of an 85-centimetre-wide window coming loose.

Foster + Partners had maintained that its role in the project was limited to the visual aspects of the design, and that it had not been involved in technical matters.

Jurors were told that in August 2017, just over a year before Ferris's death, another window panel had fallen from the same development with no changes made to the designs in response.

Prosecutor Gordon Menzies had said "it wasn't an accident waiting to happen" but "an accident waiting to happen again", reported the Guardian.

"It's reasonably practicable for clever people to do a simple thing and design a window that doesn't fall out once every year," he added, according to MyLondon.

Strong winds had blown the window wide open, with the oversailing glass clashing with the frame and prising off the hinges, Menzies told the court.

The court also heard that the windows had originally been designed to open inwards, but were changed to outward-openers to avoid clashing with an internal ceiling coffer containing wires and pipes.

"It had no effective failsafe, no reliable back-up. There were many things that could go wrong with the restrictors and if they did, consequences could be catastrophic," Menzies said of the outward-opening window design, per BBC reporting.

"We note the court's decision"

Following Ferris's death, the windows were changed back to inward-opening.

A spokesperson for Foster + Partners said: "Our thoughts remain with Mr Ferris' family, as they have since October 2018. We note the court's decision and are grateful to the jury for the time and care they have taken in considering this matter."

A spokesperson for Wintech said: "While the court has reached its conclusion, the tragedy of what happened remains. It is vital that we continue to reflect and learn, and as an industry, remain committed to strengthening standards and practices to help prevent such incidents in the future."

A spokesperson for St James Group said: "The death of Mick Ferris in 2018 was tragic. Our thoughts remain with his family and friends. We acknowledge today's verdict and will carefully consider its implications."

Dezeen has approached Lindner Prater for comment.

item.content:encoded:
Production designers Brandon Tonner-Connolly and Matt Hyland constructed sets including a "flesh palace" and a taxidermy-filled gas station to create a dreamlike world for this horror film starring Gillian Anderson.

The name of the film, Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma, nods to the lurid titles of 1970s and 80s slasher movies – a feeling the designers also wanted to evoke with the sets themselves.

The movie centres around filmmaker Kris, played by actor Hannah Einbinder, who has been tasked with reviving the fictional Camp Miasma franchise.

She travels to meet Billy, played by Anderson – the star of the cult horror film that started the Camp Miasma horror franchise – who now lives on an abandoned summer camp that featured in the first film.

Tonner-Connolly and Hyland wanted Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma, which was directed by Jane Schoenbrun, to immediately draw both Kris and the audience into Billy's self-contained world on the horror-film set.

"[It's] very much supposed to be a moment where Kris is walking into this storybook world, leaving behind the reality that we've created in the first 20 minutes of the film and entering into this storybook romance," Tonner-Connolly told Dezeen.

To create a dreamlike feeling, the designers used matte glass painting, a technique of painting on glass plates that are then placed in front of the camera. This created fantastical backgrounds, such as fairytale-like mountains that sit behind the old summer camp site.

"We knew from the very beginning that the MO of this movie wasn't 'let's set out and scare the shit out of everybody,' it was 'we should take people on the best ride possible,'" Hyland told Dezeen.

Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma was mainly shot on location using two functioning summer camps on Vancouver Island, Canada.

These were turned into the summer camps seen both in the film's contemporary timeline and the 1980s summer camp of the older Camp Miasma movies.

Vancouver Island turned out to be a treasure trove of products and props, including taxidermied animals that Tonner-Connolly and Hyland used to decorate a run-down gas station.

The sourcing of these pieces ended up feeling like a horror film in itself, according to Tonner-Connolly.

"I was just driving down a road one day and saw a faded sign on the side of the road that said 'taxidermy studio' and an arrow; I pulled off a two-lane highway onto a back road and then just drove to somebody's house," he said.

"I got out and it's completely silent, nobody around, just a workshop off in the distance and a massive wood pile," Tonner-Connolly continued.

"And I was like: 'God, actually, nobody knows where I am right now – this is a very Texas Chainsaw Massacre moment'."

Other cult horror films that inspired the designers to create the right feel for the sets included Friday the 13th, Halloween and Nightmare on Elm Street.

"For this movie's approach to period and genre, it's not really about rote memorisation of accurate details – it's more about getting ourselves into the mentality of 'if we're making a slasher in the 80s, this is what we'd have available to us'," Hyland said.

Read:

Architects will "cringe a bit" at design horrors in Backrooms says production designer

However, Tonner-Connolly and Hyland also turned to the gothic romance genre to get the romantic aspect of the film right.

"We looked at Bram Stoker's Dracula and other examples of gothic romance," Hyland said. "Also Black Narcissus and Kwaidan, an older Japanese film where everything was shot on stage, even the exteriors, so it has a very heightened, storybook reality."

Some of the designs for Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma were replicated from these older films, as a nod to the inspiration and an Easter egg for horror fans.

"There was the scene where [villain] Little Death rises out of the lake, and there was a really specific life vest rack and lifeguard chair that we had seen in one of those slasher films on the beach," Tonner-Connolly said.

"We had our construction scenic department build it exactly to what it looked like in that film, and it's very subtle in the background."

Other designs were created using more modern techniques, such as the flesh wall inside Little Death's "Flesh Palace", which was a combination of visual effects and a physical wall.

"In terms of the Flesh Palace, we created a very large portion [of the wall] near where the movie slot is," Hyland said.

"That was first drawn as concept art and then turned into a 3D mockup", he continued. "From that 3D model, we were able to further illustrate the walls and figure out the undulations – how crazy are they? How veiny? And then we were able to actually export directly from there to a robot that carves that shape out of foam."

Overall, the designers focused on creating a world that would feel real not just to the film's viewers, but also to the actors as they were moving through the sets.

"We're designing for the camera, but we're also designing for the people who are in the space with us when we're shooting it," Tonner-Connolly said.

"We need to have these small details so that we can create this fully realised world. So anybody can open any drawer, anybody can look at anything, anybody can – hopefully – step into it and get lost in this bubble and create this intimate work of art."

Other film sets recently covered on Dezeen include horror film Backrooms and the Shaker-focused drama The Testament of Ann Lee.

The photography is courtesy of Mubi.

item.content:encoded:
In this week's comments update, readers are discussing The Linhay, a family house in the Somerset countryside designed by studio Charles Gillespie Architecture.

Wrapped by a concrete colonnade, the house draws on the traditional linhay – a type of agricultural barn that is local to the region, characterised by its open-fronted form.

"Love, love, love this house!"

"This had potential, nice materials, lovely site, good references, but the design doesn't work at the level of basic proportions, composition and choice of elements," wrote Griff Ryan. "The landscape design is the nicest part."

Jessie called the project "A bit of a hodgepodge of ideas," while MKE Tom wrote, "This house has many personalities, all fighting to express themselves."

Unimpressed, JZ called it "a very upper-crusty, landed gentry vibe", while David Chase Martin said, "Even the land it sits on is embarrassed."

Though some readers were disappointed by the design, others were pleased.

"It has a vernacular banality few architects are brave enough to embrace," wrote Jb. "Well done."

Sharing their appreciation, Luke McClelland said, "A well-executed, thoughtfully designed family home. Good work Charlie."

"Love, love, love this house! Columns are a great idea and I like the differences between the facades," added Z-dog. "Great strength to the building."

What are your thoughts? Join the discussion ›

"They'll have to work harder"

Another story gaining attention this week was Decoy Font made by company Mixfont that layers two images together to trick contemporary artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots into misreading messages.

Readers shared their own experiences using the optical illusion font with different AI chatbots.

"Saved the pic and sent it to Google Gemini and it got it right on the first try," shared Fabian. "They'll have to work harder."

In response, RK said, "Odd. Did the same test on Gemini Flash Extended and it got it wrong. Also tried all the images on Claude and Gemini and they failed each time."

"I told Sol it was designed to trick it and it read it without any issues then explained it was a clever system but was easily defeatable by AI once it understood it needed to pay slightly more attention," said SgtZaddy. "It's the kind of trick that only works once, unfortunately."

Ironically, Chakras9 said, "Unfortunately, I also can't read it. I thought it said Happy Robot."

"What a time to be alive," said Bloibl . "We are already building defences against the thing we built."

To this, WJS replied, "That's different from the last five thousand years of making armour to defend against the weapons we also make how exactly?"

Have you had your say yet? Join the discussion ›

"Project of the week on Dezeen"

A project that readers could agree on was La Source Vive, a domed copper-clad concert hall in France completed by studio PCA-Stream designed "as a musical instrument".

"Project has a personality, easy to appreciate," said Marius. "However, how is the sound? With 500 seats, sound may be an issue."

Impressed, Bras Cubas wrote, "Very smart, I really like the seating and the lighting, and also the extra spaces for the technicians between the inside and outside layer."

"Looks lovely from the outside," said HP. On the same page, Design Junkie wrote, "Wow. Cool. Feels hidden away."

"Outstanding," complimented The Discreet Architect. "Project of the week on Dezeen."

What do you reckon? Join the discussion ›

item.content:encoded:
The Royal Institute of British Architects has announced its shortlist for the Neave Brown Award for Housing 2026, which includes the expansion of a 1970s housing estate with 46 homes for social rent in London.

Also in London, a landscape-led residential development spanning five brick buildings and a 100 per cent affordable housing block bordering a woodland are among this year's shortlisted projects.

A housing complex in Glasgow combining stacked maisonettes, apartments and terraced homes also made the list.

Awarded annually, the Neave Brown Award for Housing recognises the UK's best new affordable housing. It is named in honour of British social housing pioneer Neave Brown.

The three London-based projects are Rowan Court by Satish Jassal Architects, Lion Green Road by Mary Duggan Architects with RUFF Architects and Canada Water Plot K1 by Morris+Company with White Ink.

The fourth project, located in Glasgow, is St Andrew's Drive Phases 2 & 3 by Jmarchitects.

This year's jury is chaired by associate director at Witherford Watson Mann architects Helen Lee, who praised the projects' delivery of "beautiful and enduring places to live".

"This year's shortlist for the Neave Brown Award for Housing celebrates four exceptionally high-quality affordable housing projects built in the UK recently; each reflecting Neave Brown's belief in community-focused and contextually responsive architecture," Lee said.

"The jury deliberated for some time over a very strong pool of eligible projects but were unanimous in championing the shortlisted projects," she continued.

"This year's shortlisted projects each respond skilfully to the unique urban challenges of their sites, creating beautiful and enduring places to live, supporting communities to grow and evolve," Lee added.

Satish Jassal Architects' Rowan Court oversaw the expansion of a 1970s council estate in Haringey to create 31 apartments, 11 townhouses and four wheelchair-accessible homes – all of which are for social rent.

Read:

RIBA unveils Stirling Prize 2026 shortlist

In Croydon, Lion Green Road by Mary Duggan Architects and RUFF Architects provides 157 homes between five brick buildings designed to optimise access to the surrounding verdant landscape.

Morris+Company and White Ink designed the Canada Water Plot K1 development to reflect its position beside a woodland in south east London, organising its 79 homes around a central courtyard.

In Glasgow, St Andrew's Drive Phases 2 & 3 by Jmarchitects replaces a 1960s block with a collection of 120 new homes that share a green space.

The winner of the Neave Brown Award for Housing will be announced at the RIBA Stirling Prize ceremony on 15 October in London.

The RIBA also recently announced its six-strong shortlist for this year's Stirling Prize, which includes Renzo Piano Building Workshop's cube-shaped Paddington Square. It also recently named 32 buildings the best British buildings of 2026, over half of which were in London.

item.content:encoded:
Local interior studio Crissy Zhang Design has transformed the interior of the Parkhill residence in Melbourne, Australia, using arched forms and tactile materials to create a soft, calming space.

As part of the renovation of the 265-square-metre home, the studio redefined its internal spatial layout but largely retained the structure of the house.

"Rather than pursuing stark minimalism, Parkhill is a contemporary Melbourne residence shaped by softness, restraint and a quiet, modern Parisian sensibility," Crissy Zhang Design founder Crissy Zhang told Dezeen.

"Furniture and artworks are given room to breathe, with refinement expressed through proportion, rhythm and material control rather than ornament."

A series of arched openings was introduced to soften and reimagine the interior of the two-storey home.

According to Zhang, each arched opening was developed in response to a specific architectural constraint.

Some of these were used to conceal irregular structural outlines, while others integrate the existing structure but reshape the connection between rooms.

"What elevates the work is the degree of transformation achieved through restraint," Zhang said.

"The central idea was to re-form the house from within rather than rebuild it, transformed not by rebuilding its shell, but by carefully reimagining the architecture within it," she continued.

The communal spaces on the house's ground floor are visually linked by the arched openings, allowing for a more fluid circulation between a series of previously disconnected rooms.

The carefully proportioned openings also ensure privacy for spaces such as the study and the library, by establishing a dynamic spatial rhythm without defaulting to a generic open-plan design.

Read:

Century-old Melbourne corner shop transformed into family home

The improved visual connections and continuity across the kitchen, dining, living, study, library and bathing areas also allow natural light to move more freely through the plan.

The studio also carved sculptural niches into the thickened walls, using the same arched forms.

Crissy Zhang Design then added recessed timber shelving into the wall niches, which, together with custom-made cabinets, provide more storage space.

Tactile materials with muted tones were used to evoke a sense of grounding and quiet luxury. Limewashed walls, natural stone and pale timber were used to create a space that would feel warm and comforting.

Established in Melbourne in 2023, Crissy Zhang Design has completed a series of residential and retail projects.

Elsewhere in Melbourne, Kister Architects has turned a former 1910 corner shop into a family home, while MRTN Architects designed an extension for a house with a "collage" of forms in red-toned brick, metal and timber.

The photography is by Timothy Kaye.

item.content:encoded:
Canadian practice Leckie Studio has completed Twin Peaks House, which features an asymmetrical roof and silvery wood cladding that helps the building "recede among the trees".

Located in North Vancouver and designed for a young family, the Twin Peaks House sits on a sloped property dotted with trees.

Local practice Leckie Studio set out to create a dwelling that felt cohesive while allowing for variety.

"The house explores how a singular formal system can accommodate different ways of living," the studio said.

"Twin House does not rely on contrast for effect. Its discipline lies in holding variation within a controlled frame."

In plan, the 3,790-square-foot (352-square-metre) house consists of two offset squares. Atop each volume are gabled roofs that slope in opposite directions, giving the house a sculptural look.

Mature evergreen trees conceal the full silhouette. Grey-hued, vertical cedar cladding further integrates the building into the landscape.

"The richness of the silvered wood allows the house to recede among the trees or emerge subtly as light shifts across the facade," said Leckie Studio.

The base layer of the home is a cast-in-place concrete plinth that accommodates the site's slopes.

A narrow walkway lined with concrete walls leads to the front door. Inside, a stairwell sits between the home's two volumes, acting as "hinge".

"From here, the house expands in one direction and contracts in the other," the team said.

"One half expands toward openness and collective use – the other turns inward toward rest and privacy."

To the west is the expansive area – an open-plan kitchen, dining area and living room.

A broad, horizontal window provides eye-level views of tree trunks and understorey. Overhead, a sloped ceiling rises gently and culminates in a circular oculus.

The other half of the house contains two bedrooms and is meant to feel more enclosed.

"The outer geometry remains consistent, yet the interior becomes more contained," the team said. "Openings are narrower and more deliberate, light is indirect."

One of the bedrooms features a circular skylight and a small loft.

"A loft occupies the apex of one gable, overlooking the living space below," the team said. "Its footprint is modest, but its position reinforces the sectional continuity of the volume."

The house also has a lower level with an office, gym, laundry room and garage.

Read:

Leckie Studio designs penthouse inside BIG's Vancouver skyscraper

For interior spaces, the team used a restrained material palette that "allows shifts in light – morning, overcast, dusk – to register without distraction".

Finishes include polished concrete floors, white drywall and oak veneers on custom millwork.

Overall, the building's design aims to "prevent symmetry from becoming inert".

"The two volumes share proportion and material language, but shifts in aperture, ceiling height and sectional organisation create distinct spatial conditions," the team said.

"Rather than expressing contrast outwardly, the project contains it within the shared shells."

Other projects by Leckie Studio include a timber-clad house in British Columbia that frames mountain views and a penthouse apartment inside a Vancouver skyscraper designed by BIG.

Media personality and former Queer Eye host Tan France has released an 18-piece homeware collection with Singapore brand Castlery, which marks his first foray into furniture design.

France, who formerly guided fashion transformations on the Netflix show Queer Eye, told Dezeen the Castlery x Tan France Collection was informed by his British and South Asian heritage.

"I designed my current home, including some of the furniture in my home, and had the most incredible experience doing so," France told Dezeen. "Some of the items in this Castlery collection were items I wanted to make for my home but hadn't gotten to it yet."

The collection ranges from a modular Kagan sofa and an egg-like accent chair to the brightly coloured Anika table lamp and side tables informed by traditional wood turning.

Warm oak wood was used throughout the collection, along with a palette of earthy oranges and greens.

A scalloped arch can also be found in much of the detailing – a motif that France used to guide the overall collection as a nod to his South Asian roots.

"I mostly wanted to focus on a scalloped arch," said France. "It's something that is seen all over South Asia, and a muted version over all of England."

"So that was the jumping-off point, and it helped me keep the collection cohesive, as there was a clear North Star."

Read:

Pamela Anderson releases rattan furniture line informed by seaside childhood

France said he came to the design experience with ideas already in mind and that his experience in fashion design made it an enjoyable, and somewhat similar, process.

"It felt so exciting designing homeware as opposed to what I've lived most of my life designing, which was clothes," France said.

"Honestly, with such comfort with designing clothing, the design of home goods felt quite natural, as I understand fabrications, colour story and function," he continued. "It's not too dissimilar a process."

Other objects in the collection include decorative vases, a low tea table with scalloped arches etched into its legs, and wool rugs.

France says bedroom furniture may be next.

"If they have me back, I'd love to design a bed and other bedroom furniture," he said. "I'd also love to design tableware, as I'm a very keen dinner host."

The collection joins other homeware designs recently launched by celebrities who have paired up with furniture brands to help guide the design process and manufacturing.

These include a rattan furniture collection by Pamela Anderson and Los Angeles furniture company Olive Ateliers and a collection by actor and comedian Julio Torres and furniture brand Sabai, which was informed by the experience of immigrating to New York City.

The photography is courtesy of Tan France x Castlery.

item.content:encoded:
Gently curving rooflines and an asymmetrical heart-shaped stairwell characterise this multi-generational home in Ahmedabad, designed by local practices Studio Saransh and Iksoi Studio.

Named LJ House, the four-storey, 585-square-metre home was completed for a family of six on a compact urban plot, with the brief calling for an adaptable layout to accommodate changing needs.

Studio Saransh and Iksoi Studio drew upon the social and spatial principles of Ahmedabad's traditional pols – gated clusters of wooden, climate-responsive residences – maximising communal space and utilising passive cooling.

"The influence of pol houses extends beyond planning – we were interested in the underlying social and climatic intelligence of pol houses, rather than just their formal language," Studio Saransh associate partner Mansi Mistry told Dezeen.

Finished in earthy plaster with selective stone detailing, the building's form is softened by gently curving roofs along the upper levels. According to the studio, these curved roofs were shaped to reduce structural load and minimise horizontal surfaces that are likely to accumulate dust in Ahmedabad.

"As the design evolved, the curves became a way of completing the building's silhouette, breaking the rigidity of the stacked volume while preserving its monolithic character," said Mistry.

Designed around collective living, the ground floor contains an interconnected living room, dining area and kitchen that open onto a series of peripheral courtyards, extending the shared spaces outdoors.

A high boundary wall encloses the ground floor, maintaining privacy and buffering the home from street noise.

Set out in a "vertically stacked framework", LJ House is centred around a sculptural staircase that organises movement between its floors.

Designed to encourage interaction between family members, each discontinuous flight of stairs opens directly onto a shared living space, referencing the circulation patterns of Ahmedabad's pol houses. Above, an asymmetrical heart-shaped void draws daylight into the centre of the house.

Read:

SpaceDNA arranges split levels of Indian home around rust-orange staircase

"The geometry of the stairwell was almost a coincidence," said Mistry. "It emerged through the iterative process of balancing circulation, daylight and maintaining visual connections across multiple levels."

"As the stair wrapped around the central void, its changing profile naturally resulted in an asymmetrical form that resembles a heart when viewed from below," Mistry described.

LJ House's first and second floors each contain a cluster of two bedrooms arranged around a shared living space, designed to allow different generations to occupy separate floors in the future.

Bedrooms were intended to primarily be places for rest, allowing more floor space to be allocated to communal living areas.

"Private bedrooms were intentionally kept compact, containing only the functions necessary for rest," said Mistry.

"By keeping private spaces purely utilitarian, the space saved was reallocated to generous shared living areas on each floor," Mistry stated.

Throughout the interior, the architects used a pared-back palette combining muted matte finishes and continuous stone flooring, while locally sourced teak furniture introduces warmth and contrast.

"The material palette was intentionally restrained to reinforce the idea of the house as a continuous carved volume rather than a collection of individual rooms," said Mistry.

The sculptural staircase culminates in a partially enclosed roof terrace on the top floor.

Designed for Ahmedabad's hot climate, the house combines double-layered cavity walls, deep-set windows and limited openings in the external facade to reduce heat gain, while courtyards and internal voids allow for natural ventilation.

Other Indian houses recently featured on Dezeen include a courtyard house by Spacefiction wrapped in perforated brickwork and a home in Tamil Nadu by Meister Varma Architects that is built from salvaged stone.

The photography is by Ishita Sitwala.

Project credits:

Architect: Studio Saransh and Iksoi Studio
Interior design: Studio Saransh
Principal architect: Mansi Mistry

item.content:encoded:
Dutch studio MVRDV has revealed designs for the Bihailou Art Village, a cultural development in Shenzhen, China, set to comprise a stack of colourful volumes.

Currently under construction in the Shatoujiao neighbourhood near the Hong Kong border, the 6,500-square-metre complex will contain cultural and retail spaces, including a museum and a double-height theatre, within its geometrically shaped volumes.

MVRDV conceptualised the proposal as a "vertical village", drawing on nearby homes and buildings for its assorted colours, shapes and materials.

"The joy of this design lies in its contradictions," studio co-founder Winy Maas said.

"It looks complex, but the idea of one space for every function is really quite simple."

"Though it may look like something that has never been done before, it is in fact a remix of the surrounding village: combining the colours, materials, and shapes of both its neighbours and the restaurant that once stood on this site," Maas added.

Rather than housing the programmes within one large volume, MVDRV opted for individual "houses" that could be tailored to their respective programmes.

Each volume has also been designed with its own entrance and will be connected to its neighbours via an external network of staircases, escalators and ramps.

This way, the studio explains, each programme can operate independently and determine its own opening hours.

The spaces will include a performance theatre, held within a spacious, double-height volume overlooking a plaza through a floor-to-ceiling opening.

Retractable chairs will feature in the space, allowing it to transform into an exhibition hall. Shops and restaurants will be held within the complex's smaller blocks.

Read:

MVRDV wins competition for "new world wonder" in the Netherlands

Renders of the Bihailou Art Village reveal a combination of boxy, rounded and pitched volumes finished in various types of cladding.

A landscaped plaza will wrap around its ground level, complemented by a series of "freely accessible" roof terraces atop the volumes.

"The design is imbued with a kind of civic generosity, not only in the form of its permanent accessibility and public roof terraces, but also on the ground level, where the stacked shape creates overhangs where people can shelter from sun and rain," the studio said.

MVRDV was recently named winner of a competition to design a "new world wonder" in Rotterdam, the Netherlands.

Elsewhere, the studio wrapped Beijing roof tiles around a flagship store for Urban Revivo in Beijing and topped a "polite yet radical" housing block in Eindhoven with angular roofs.

The renders are courtesy of MVRDV.

item.content:encoded:
The lily pads that float on the Kerala backwaters were the inspiration for this multi-generational apartment renovation in Mumbai by local studio The Act of Quad.

Poetically named A Borrowed Memory, the apartment is characterised by continuous green flooring designed to echo the interconnected lakes, rivers and lagoons known as the Kerala backwaters in southern India.

Priyanka Itadkar and Falguni Bhatia of The Act of Quad were drawn to the backwaters' lily pads when crafting the interior, which they said was designed to feel like "arriving at the edge of a still body of water".

This involved replacing rigid corners with curved, lime-washed walls across the home, which was renovated for a multi-generational family made up of a couple and two elderly grandparents.

Various bespoke furniture pieces in the living space were finished in subtle organic shapes, including undulating dining chairs and a door-mounted green sculpture that looks like a large curled leaf.

The studio also designed a delicate lily pad-like coffee table from clay, which was then moulded and cast in fibre. The table's jade sheen was embellished with delicate resin droplets to recall the stillness of the backwaters.

A sofa was draped in light green fabric, offering a soft antidote to an intricate hand-carved timber pillar sourced from Kerala as another homage to the state.

"Various pieces borrow the form of lily pads, but stop short of becoming literal representations," explained Itadkar and Bhatia. "The intention was never to recreate a landscape, but to allow fragments of it to quietly inhabit the home."

Elsewhere in the apartment, the grandparents' bedroom was designed to be the most peaceful space in the house, with muted tones and handcrafted timber furniture to complement the curved walls.

Rounded windowpanes, mirrors and headboards characterise multiple rooms in another subtle nod to the shape of lily pads.

The studio took care to adapt the home to fit the needs of its residents, who range in age, which included introducing a curved wall in the dining room to enlarge its adjoining bathroom to make it accessible for wheelchairs.

The younger couple's green-hued bedroom features a custom wardrobe that conceals an entire walk-in dressing space between two sliding timber panels.

In the living space, a concealed home theatre system was fitted in lieu of a permanent television on display, to encourage the sociable atmosphere of traditional multi-generational Indian homes.

Itadkar and Bhatia said that despite the modest plan of the single-floor apartment, they were determined not to compromise on standout touches including space-saving devices and bespoke furniture.

Read:

Cobalt-blue accents brighten interior of family apartment in Thane

"The reality of Indian cities is one of increasingly compact homes, and we find that challenge far more compelling than designing without limits," reflected the studio founders.

"Luxury today lies in creating spaces that are deeply personal, emotionally resonant and built around the lives of the people who inhabit them."

Founded in 2019, The Act of Quad has completed various other projects in Mumbai, including their self-designed studio in a former library and another multi-generational home arranged across a high-rise.

The photography is by Nayan Soni.

item.content:encoded:
Architect Charles Holland, academic Catharine Rossi and design studio Local Works have fabricated a table from materials harvested within a 40-mile radius of Canterbury, UK.

Named Harvest Moon, the table was designed to investigate the potential of local biomaterials, while evoking the ideals of gathering associated with harvest rituals.

"The table explores not just the materials we use but the attitudes and rituals around them," Holland told Dezeen.

"Everything comes from a 40-mile radius of Canterbury and that includes the tools that are used to assemble it, such as mallets and hammers made from apple tree wood and pegs made from chestnut wood."

The table was predominantly made from biomaterials including chalk, chestnut timbers, bark peelings, dug-up apple trees, combined with agricultural industrial waste products such as baling twine and pallet straps.

Its top was cast from chalk, along with other waste materials to form a terrazzo effect, while the legs were made from apple tree branches.

Read:

Charles Holland and RASKL add colourful contemporary bandstand to Mitcham Fair Green

"The biggest challenge was casting the top segments, the process of which involved a refinement of the technique by Local Works in their workshop," said Holland.

"The chalk was cast around a simple chestnut timber frame with embedded apple wood 're-bars' and is really a shell, rather than a solid object. The shell got thinner and the pieces lighter as the process went on due to a greater confidence in the materials."

Throughout the design, the team aimed to ensure that the materials and construction process were visible, which contributed to the overall aesthetic.

"The table is made from gathered materials and it visually expresses the ad-hoc nature of that…materials are bound together, used as supports and props or 'rebars' or as the basis of dyes or colouring," said Holland.

"The table top is cast chalk with other materials mixed in, including bark and wood chipping and baling twine, like a form of terrazzo," he continued.

"The earthiness of some parts is deliberately contrasted with brightly coloured binding which is both practical – the colours provide a key to the order in which the table is assembled – and decorative, allowing us to enjoy and express the contrasts between them."

As the table was designed as a research project, it will be disassembled and transported to various locations where it will be reassembled as a social activity.

"The core concept of the table is harvest, an idea of designing and making using gathered materials coupled with a related idea of ritual and social gathering," explained Holland.

"Each time the table is made it is a social gathering, like a barn raising."

Along with the table, the team created a publication that contains instructions and drawings of how to assemble the table, along with a musical score to accompany it.

"Each time it has been assembled the ritual changes slightly and the music evolves too," Holland said.

"The table itself is an active part of the dissemination because it will travel and its assembly involves a physical and conceptual interaction with it."

The publication also contains essays and a "guide for hosting a harvest gathering".

"We learnt a lot about the materials, about a collaborative process of design, and an open-ended one too," said Holland.

"But we also learned a lot about the processes of the two businesses we worked with, how growing, farming and coppicing is impacted by a mix of policy, economics, consumer taste, climate change and a host of other factors that are determining why our landscape is the way it is and how it is changing."

Holland and Rossi both teach at UCA Canterbury. Holland is the founder of Charles Holland Architects, which recently created a contemporary bandstand at Mitcham Fair Green and a colourful extension to a Victorian terraced house.

The photography is by Charles Holland, unless stated.

item.content:encoded:
With the recent release of plans to build on top of Eero Saarinen's terminal building at Dulles International Airport, we take a look at old and new controversies surrounding significant works of architecture and their preservation across the US.

Preserving historic architecture is no easy task given ageing buildings, lack of funding and the lucrative nature of new development.

From a Tadao Ando beach house gutted by musician Kanye West, to Frank Lloyd Wright's only realised skyscraper and Donald Trump's many renovation projects around Washington DC, the legal battles below showcase the often bitter fights that ensue over preserving architecture

Some of the projects have been completely renovated and refreshed, while others are scheduled for demolition, but most are suspended between the two – and have been for years.

Read on below for 11 contentious architectural preservation battles across the US.

The White House East Wing, Washington DC

The East Wing of the White House was demolished in October 2025 to make room for a giant ballroom promoted by president Donald Trump.

Preservationists pushed back on the plans, with various judges issuing injunctions to stop the building, despite approval of the new designs by local regulatory bodies. As of July 2026, construction will reportedly include an expansive underground security complex.

Questions about the legality of the demolition and construction are still being worked out in the courts.

Find out more about the White House East Wing ›

The Vaillancourt Fountain, California, by Armand Vaillancourt

This peculiar fountain in San Francisco was ruled a hazard in November 2025 by the San Francisco Arts Commission, which voted to dismantle it in anticipation of renovations to the surrounding plaza.

Despite the outcry from locals, the city began to take down the fountain earlier this year, but not before it briefly caught fire due to debris catching flame from a construction blow torch.

Find out more about the Vaillancourt Fountain ›

Dallas City Hall, Texas, by IM Pei

Late last year, the Dallas city government voted to explore relocating operations from its 1970s brutalist city hall building designed by architect IM Pei, where it currently resides, citing the building's age and cost of maintenance. A move would cast the future of the iconic structure in uncertainty.

The debate to remain in the building or relocate has sparked much local debate, with reports stating that the voting council is starkly divided.

Find out more about the Dallas City Hall ›

550 Madison skyscraper, New York, by Philip Johnson and John Burgee

After the iconic New York skyscraper sat vacant, architecture studio Snøhetta proposed a renovation that would see parts of the structure clad in glass.

The initial scheme proposed a multi-storey glass block to replace the tower's base, but after the building was granted landmark status shortly, Snøhetta pared back the design and conserved the entirety of the facade.

The studio completed the toned-down renovation in 2022.

Find out more about 550 Madison skyscraper ›

Miami Marine Stadium, Florida, by Hilario Candela 

An ongoing preservation saga has plagued Miami Marine Stadium since its closure in 1992. Since then, it has remained vacant and graffitied on its unique site where it sprawls out over a local harbour.

Conservation group Docomomo selected it as one of the most under-threat buildings in America in 2022, and Miami locals will vote to approve an operator for the stadium in the hopes of conserving it during primary elections in August, according to the Miami Herald.

Find out more about Miami Marine Stadium ›

Portland Municipal Services Building, Oregon, by Michael Graves

Michael Graves' 1982 Portland Municipal Services Building in Portland was one of the first buildings in the US to kickstart the preservation of postmodern architecture.

In 2014, the building came under threat of demolition, but with the help of advocates, including from Graves himself, Portland city council eventually decided on an extensive renovation and the building reopened in 2020.

Find out more about Portland Municipal Services Building ›

Price Tower, Oklahoma, by Frank Lloyd Wright

In late 2024, Frank Lloyd Wright's only skyscraper underwent a contentious legal battle between a local owner and The Frank Lloyd Wright Conservancy, when the latter discovered the "unapproved" sale of original furniture from the interior.

Litigation was recently settled in March 2026 after a new owner purchased the property with plans to renovate the building and operate it as a hotel with residences, a rooftop bar and a ground-floor restaurant.

Find out more about Price Tower ›

The Kennedy Center, Washington, DC, by Edward Durell Stone

The John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts in Washington DC is the subject of ongoing controversy after Donald Trump ousted its leadership in February 2025 and proposed an overhaul of the exterior. Trump also affixed his own name to the building, which was later removed.

There is an ongoing back and forth about the president's legal right to reshape the building, and groups such as the AIA have joined a lawsuit against the government in hopes of preserving the original design.

Find out more about The Kennedy Center ›

Victor Lundy House, Texas, by Victor Lundy 

A group of preservationists including the Texas Historical Foundation, Houston Mod, Docomomo US and Preservation Houston won a hard-fought battle to save American architect Victor Lundy's personal residence in Houston, Texas late last year.

With the support of the group, buyers Dan and Carol Price purchased the house, saving it from demolition. Preservation Houston says the plan is to "restore the property and explore possibilities for its continued use and preservation".

Find out more about Victor Lundy House ›

Elgin Mental Health Center Medical and Surgical building, Illinois, by Bertrand Goldberg

The circular Elgin Mental Health Center Medical and Surgical Building outside of Chicago was being eyed for demolition early last year after decades of disuse.

As of now, there is no widely reported timeline for the demolition, but the building is "worth preserving" according to Geoffrey Goldberg, son of building architect Bertrand Goldberg.

Find out more about the Elgin Mental Health Center Medical and Surgical Building ›

Malibu house, California, by Tadao Ando

A Malibu beach house by Japanese architect Tadao Ando was stripped down to its concrete structure by musician Ye and wife Bianca Censori in 2024.

Ye sold the structure after failing to convert it into a "bunker" as intended, and the current owner is struggling to sell the building before it forecloses, according to Architectural Digest.

Find out more about the Tadao Ando Malibu house ›

item.content:encoded:
International architecture studio SOM has released designs of the 20-storey 934 Central Street data centre in Kansas City, USA, with a facade configured to "feel at home within its downtown context".

The 20-storey skyscraper will be built in the heart of Kansas City on a 0.23-acre site that is currently occupied by the Western Newspaper Union Building.

Developed by Miami-based Revitalization Unlimited, the structure will incorporate floors for data systems, cooling systems, and power generation, all arrayed vertically, a marked departure from the massive horizontal structures that have dominated the news cycle in the wake of the AI boom.

"A vertical closed loop"

"Unlike conventional data centers, which typically occupy large, horizontal footprints, 934 Central Street envisions a vertical data center for a dense downtown setting, closer to where people live and work," said a spokesperson for SOM.

"The proposal stacks data floors, power infrastructure, cooling systems, and public amenities within a 20-story tower on a compact 0.23-acre site, creating a vertical closed loop of power, water, and cooling."

The structure will feature an earth-coloured masonry facade with large panes of glass, even on floors dedicated to the data modules. It will have an external core allowing for more room in the interior of the skyscraper.

On ground level, SOM has planned for 4,700 square feet (436 square metres) of shops.

The commercial element was designed with the relatively standard cladding system to make the skyscraper align with the urban context, according to SOM.

"Designed to feel at home within its downtown context, the building draws from the vertical proportions, repetitive bays, and masonry character of surrounding commercial buildings," said SOM.

Increasing data centre reliance

Likely in response to recent uproar about water and energy usage in data centers, the studio has included plans for on-site power generation, reportedly from natural gas cells. A diagram of the skyscraper supplied by SOM states that the power system is "100 per cent independent from the grid".

It also states that the water will be internally cycled through equipment on the upper floors, with evaporative cooling elements shown as a feature at the bulkhead.

SOM claimed that the proximity to the urban systems that will likely utilise the data centre's output is a reason for its location.

"As cities around the world become increasingly reliant on data centers, locating this infrastructure within urban areas offers both efficient proximity to the industries and networks it serves and an opportunity for these buildings to contribute positively to surrounding communities," said the studio.

The structure also answers a question raised by many of the massive data centres going up across the country – what will happen to these structures if the demand for computation decreases?

"The tower is also configured to adapt over time, with a side core, regular structural grid, and generous floor-to-floor heights that support future conversion to residential, office, or mixed-use space as technological needs evolve," said SOM.

However, there has been community pushback, with local outlets reporting locals pushing back on grounds of the "speculative" nature of the project and the potential for urban heat island effects, which are reportedly exacerbated by data centres.

Read:

Plant-covered Rio AI City set to be Latin America's largest data centre

Locals also expressed concern over the demolition of the Western Newspaper Union Building, with the City Planning Commission scheduled to review the project today, 5 August 2026.

Recently, Gensler designed a massive hyperscale data centre in Utah and a data centre was approved as part of the Truman Brewery development in east London.

item.content:encoded:
A vast grid of red scaffolding surrounds The Reclaimed Pavilion, a temporary events space in India designed by local studio Kanan Modi Associates using materials that were salvaged from local construction sites.

Commissioned by real estate firm Jayabheri Group for a rapidly developing neighbourhood in Hyderabad, the 1,500-square-metre pavilion contains work and events spaces alongside a show home for a nearby apartment block, The Pinnacle.

Given its temporary nature, Kanan Modi Associates looked to use salvaged and repurposed materials wherever possible. This included gabion walls made from construction debris, bricks made from excavated earth and reclaimed corrugated metal sheets, all assembled to be easily dismantled.

Surrounding the entire site is a gridded framework made from repurposed scaffolding, which has been painted a deep shade of red and used to support a series of zigzagging jute fabric canopies that shade its external areas.

"Rather than asking what new materials could be introduced, every design decision began with the question: what already exists that can be given a second life?" Kanan Modi Associates founder Kana Modi told Dezeen.

"Equally important was planning for the pavilion's eventual dismantling. The scaffolding system will return to construction use, corrugated metal sheets will be reused, and the excavated earth blocks can return to the ground as fill."

Entering into a pale brick-paved reception area with a sunken pit at its centre, The Reclaimed Pavilion is organised as a row of flexible gathering and events spaces, lined by more compartmentalised, privates spaces for work and meetings.

Dividing the pavilion's three main spaces are large gabion walls made from construction debris, which extend beyond the pavilion's edges to help shade and separate its external areas.

Read:

Dum-Dum Lab constructs lakeside pavilion as environmental classroom

"A series of open gathering areas, shaded seating zones and flexible event spaces flow around a central water body, encouraging movement and informal interaction," Modi told Dezeen.

"The flexible layout allows the pavilion to seamlessly accommodate art exhibitions, talks, performances, community events and informal gatherings, adapting to a diverse range of public programmes."

The central spaces are flanked by a stepped steel deck and shallow L-shaped pool that wraps the pavilion's southwestern edge, and a more enclosed external plaza to the north, which is shaded by the scaffolding canopy and overlooks another pool of water.

Atop these pools of water, the scaffolding grid is echoed by a grid of pale concrete stepping stones, which were cast in-situ in an irregular checkerboard layout.

At its western end, the show flat sits separated from the main space of the pavilion, occupying a contrasting white volume that is also encased within the pavilion's scaffolding.

Other projects in India that have given a new life to salvaged construction waste include the Belgaluru studio of design practice Multitude of Sins, which made use of scrap metal and acrylic sheets, chains and even door knobs.

The photography is by Fernando Guerra.

item.content:encoded:
Architecture studio MAD has unveiled Shenzhen Bay Culture Square in China, a design museum formed of stone-like volumes perched atop an undulating green roof.

Situated in Houhai in Shenzhen's Nanshan District, MAD designed the museum to be a hub for design and culture as well as a coastal public space for city residents to enjoy.

"Much of my work is guided by the same question: can public space be more open and equal?" said MAD founder Ma Yansong.

"Shenzhen is a young, efficient city, and this site was entirely reclaimed from the sea," he continued. "How can our design turn ancient nature into people's imagination of the future, and make a large cultural building feel intimate, in service of human experience?"

Flanked by a cluster of skyscrapers on one side and Talent Park on the other side, the Shenzhen Bay Culture Square contains exhibition galleries, education spaces, a design library and a multifunctional theatre.

An undulating green roof spans over the site, concealing much of the museum space below ground and providing winding routes between the city and coastline.

Atop the green roof are boulder-like volumes clad in polished granite, which decrease in height from a 28-metre-tall gallery at the city end of the site, to a long, low-slung domed gallery positioned towards the adjacent park.

The building was designed to lie low in the landscape to stay out of the flight path of migratory birds travelling the East Asian-Australasian Flyway.

Read:

MAD clads bulbous science museum with silver-toned polymer panels in China

"By placing the building volumes beneath the landscape, the project leaves the ground to nature, creating an open waterfront park where people can freely walk, explore, and linger," said MAD.

"Visitors enter from every direction, climb the gentle slopes, follow the winding roof paths, and reach lookouts over the bay."

In the subterranean galleries, the concrete structure was left exposed, with lights and services tucked into the ceiling.

A ring-shaped atrium encircles one of the stone-like volumes, connecting the underground galleries and drawing daylight in.

A shallow pool sits at the centre of the site, and an outdoor plaza was designed to host outdoor performances, art markets and festivals.

Native species of planting populate the roof, and the landscaping abutting the wetland area of the adjacent park gradually steps down towards the shore, designed to blend into it rather than forming a hard border.

Other projects recently completed by MAD in China include a bulbous science museum in Haikou and a curving headquarters building in Shenzhen.

The photography is courtesy of MAD.

item.content:encoded:
Asca Studio and Relief Gallery joined forces to create the interiors of the Ómós guesthouse outside Abbeyleix, Ireland, which was converted from a ruin into a welcoming space filled with tactile materials.

The 16-room guesthouse is located in a formerly dilapidated Victorian house that was renovated by local studio Ryan W Kennihan Architects.

It also has a dedicated restaurant, set in a new building that was designed by the same studio and informed by Irish farmsteads.

Interior architects Asca Studio and Relief Gallery were challenged to create an interior that would make the separate spaces feel like two halves of a whole.

"Although both the guesthouse and restaurant carry the same spirit of hospitality central to how clients and staff move throughout the space, the two concepts naturally differ," Asca Studio co-founder Cassandra Bradfield told Dezeen.

"However, material palettes as well as small systems like integrated symbols within the hardware, furniture pieces, and woodwork create a sense of internal symbology and consistency throughout."

The two studios used tactile materials throughout Ómós' interior, contrasting local stone with plaster and wood.

"The foundational materials are Kilkenny limestone, ash, and lime plaster: the limestone adds weight and longevity, the ash character and warmth, and the lime plaster reflects light and absorbs sound because it is so textural," Relief Gallery founder Rebecca Norberg told Dezeen.

"The limestone was used on surfaces exposed heavily to the elements and wear, for example outdoors, on public entrance floors, vanity basins and shower trays, whilst we used wood to contrast this on more protected floors, joinery, furniture, doors and accessories."

As the guesthouse part of Ómós was "essentially a ruin", according to Norberg, the designers worked to preserve and reinstate typical period details from the Victorian house.

These included fireplaces as well as skirtings and mouldings, with the layout of the three front rooms also recreated.

The overall concept behind the guesthouse was to both celebrate its surroundings outside Abbeyleix, Ireland's oldest estate town, and make it stand out.

"Ómós is an Irish word meaning homage, duty and respect – the brief was to celebrate people, place and produce, and make the guesthouse and restaurant a destination," Norberg said.

"We wanted it to feel like nothing else in Ireland and, at the same time, deeply familiar to anyone who grew up there."

Read:

Reds shingles create "sense of personality and wonder" at Cucu cabin by Studio Bucky

Asca and Relief Gallery also added new details that fit the historic feel of the building, including a stone basin in an entryway.

"The stone basin was a new addition to the space, which functions as a 'boot wash' and filling station for both guests and staff to use," Bradfield explained.

Ómós has a warm, muted colour palette, with soft beige and green hues taking centre stage. This was inspired by the surrounding nature of County Laois in central Ireland.

"The colour palette is a mixture of tones directly taken from the site, inspired to reflect or enhance the natural light coming in, and lean into the energy of each specific space," Bradfield said.

"For instance, one suite and ensuite located in close proximity to the main garden features about 10 shades of green and blue taken directly from the vignette you see outside, and then there's a sunny yellow suite located at the front of the property that mirrors the light streaming in."

For the furniture, Bradfield and Norberg sourced vernacular vintage pieces, which were combined with custom designs by their studios and work by Irish craftsmen, as well as Scandinavian furniture.

"Standouts include the hedge chairs in the restaurant lounge, the dining chairs by Michael Murphy and De La Espada's Arts and Crafts Sideboard in Suite 01," she said.

Overall, the designers believe the final design fulfilled the vision that they set out to create.

"Irish visitors tell us they have never experienced anything like it here, and that, at the same time, the breakfast room reminds them of their grandmother's cottage kitchen, and that's how we know the design works," Norberg concluded.

Other recent Irish projects featured on Dezeen include an elevated extension in Dublin and an off-grid cabin clad in red shingles.

item.content:encoded:
Researchers in China have created a textile from living mycelium that is self-cleaning, near self-repairing and can be coloured or made UV protective through "plug-and-play" add-ons of different fungi or yeast.

The breakthrough from the researchers at the Shenzhen Institutes of Advanced Technology is a type of engineered living material (ELM) – a material built off living organisms that stay active even after they're fabricated into their final form.

This distinguishes it from most contemporary uses of mycelium, which involve drying and effectively killing the fungus to produce a stable, non-growing material that has become a popular emerging alternative to plastic packaging and vinyl.

By working with living but dormant cordyceps militaris fungus instead, the researchers have been able to take advantage of its biological functions. The result is a material that is self-renewing and responsive to its environment, in ways that could one day transform architecture and clothing – as seen in a prototype dress created together with material innovation company Peelshere.

It can also be adapted by mixing in other fungi or yeast, lead researcher Ke Li and her team detail in a paper in the peer-reviewed journal Science Advances.

In it, they describe a "programmable fungal platform" where mycelium is treated like a modular system, with the sheet material forming a base structure and extra biological abilities, such as colour and UV resistance, becoming "plug-and-play" add-ons via other organisms.

This gets their textile closer to the self-repair, environmental responsiveness and controllable functionality that is the promise of engineered living materials, they argue.

"While synthetic biology has greatly expanded the functional capabilities of ELMs, a persistent challenge lies in integrating autonomous structural assembly with sustained biological activity at macroscopic scales," the scientists write.

"Achieving such integration is essential for practical applications, from adaptive textiles to architectural biomaterials, where mechanical robustness, spatial uniformity and scalable fabrication must converge with engineered biological function."

Read:

Algae "biocells" powered by photosynthesis could replace disposable batteries

The ELM's self-renewing and semi-repairing functionality comes from the mycelium base structure. Following drying at 45 degrees, the material is not quite living and not quite dead, but instead in a "low-metabolic, dormant-like state", Li told Dezeen, meaning it is not actively growing.

However, new growth can be triggered by applying a nutrient solution of potato water, leading the dormant mycelium to germinate, send out new fungal filaments and renew the material's surface.

When this nutrient solution is applied over a hole, along with a small patch of fresh fungus, it triggers the living cells to grow across the gap, seamlessly repairing the surface without any adhesives or stitching. The material is also naturally self-cleaning, as it is hydrophobic.

The blue colour and UV resistance, meanwhile, come from brewer's yeast – also known as saccharomyces cerevisiae – and aspergillus niger fungus, respectively. These are mixed in with the cordyceps militaris at the beginning and simply co-cultured, avoiding the need for genetic engineering.

A prototype dress has been made out of the scientists' material by Berlin-based Peelshere, whose founder YouYang Song is a friend of Li's. Song developed the conceptual and aesthetic design of the dress, while her China-based colleague Ruochen Wang took care of the cutting and construction.

The dress features several versions of the material, including some co-cultured with brewer's yeast for the consistently self-pigmented blue shade in the body of the garment.

Li told Dezeen that the material is suitable for applications such as conceptual fashion, accessories, decorative textile surfaces, exhibition pieces and biodegradable packaging.

"Its distinctive surface texture, biological colouring, controlled repair and biodegradability may be particularly useful in applications where visual expression and a defined product lifetime are important," she said.

"Further improvements in durability, moisture resistance, safety and manufacturing consistency would be needed before it could be considered for routine clothing or permanent architectural use."

Peelsphere's main product is a plant-based and waterproof leather alternative made of fruit peels and algae.

Photography by Ke Li.

item.content:encoded:
Local studio River Architects has designed a wood-clad structure to Passive House standards, orienting gabled volumes around a pond in New York's Hudson Valley.

Known as the China Pond Passive House, the 4,318-square-foot (400-square-metre) home sits on a wooded 2.2-acre property in Carmel, New York.

River Architects, which is based in nearby Cold Spring, completed the house in November 2025, replacing an earlier residence with a similar footprint.

The studio built the new home from the ground up but didn't approach the site as a blank slate.

"We wanted to maintain that sense of evolution in the new house, a decision which also helps break up the overall form so it doesn't seem overwhelming," James Hartford, principal and partner of River Architects, told Dezeen.

"The result is a playful push and pull in massing, resulting in unusual in-between places and quirky angles."

Connecting with the site's existing infrastructure and stonework, the house works in dialogue with its surrounding trees and views of the water, capturing the spirit of the original house – a collection of spaces that balance a sense of retreat with the encouragement to gather.

In order to echo the additive nature of camp buildings and reduce the scale of the house, the massing is broken into a series of smaller volumes.

Two gabled forms – a two-level bar that faces east and west and a three-level bar that is rotated slightly – are joined by a flat-roofed wedge.

The forms are wrapped in reclaimed cypress and Douglas fir above the native stone foundation that is partially embedded in the sloped site.

Inside, the team worked to recreate the feeling of the original library in the great room to be both intimate and expansive for entertaining, with views and daylight. Private sleeping spaces are ganged to the southern side of the house, while the communal areas blend between the central and northern portions.

The lower level is more informal with recreation space, a sauna and access to a large deck that mimics the terrace on the main level.

"A central stone chimney serves as the physical and social heart of the home, organizing the primary living and outdoor spaces while anchoring views and activity around it," Hartford said.

"The house opens to the landscape, balancing expansive lake views with moments of privacy and shelter."

 

In order to achieve Passive House certification, sustainable elements were embedded in the project from the outset.

The house features a highly insulated and airtight building envelope, triple-pane glazing, careful solar orientation and shading strategies that reduce energy demand while improving comfort.

The locally sourced wood reduced carbon impact and maintenance, while active systems – all-electric heat pumps, energy recovery ventilation and infrastructure for renewable energy generation – contribute to the performance.

"Together, these measures enabled the project to achieve Phius certification and provide exceptional indoor comfort with significantly reduced operational energy use and no fossil fuel use," the studio said.

Other recently built single-family Passive Houses include a retrofitted terrace house in Queens by CO Adaptive, a courtyard home in Chile by Paralelo Transversal and a retrofitted Victorian home with a "fabric first" approach in London by GS Architecture.

item.content:encoded:
New York studios Schlaich Bergermann Partner and Snøhetta have replaced an ageing bridge in Upstate New York with a steel half-arch span that is mounted on one side of a gorge and cantilevers across to the other side.

The Sentry Bridge replaces a decaying structure of the same name located in Watkins Glen State Park in the Finger Lakes region of New York.

The bridge is wedged between two cavernous rock walls among the park's twisting, mossy trails that navigate along Watkins Glen gorge, and overlooks a low riverbed at the base of a waterfall.

It marks the beginning of the gorge path, and, according to the team, "sets a tone for adventure".

"The bridge and pathways honour the histories and craft traditions of the gorge, protect unique cliff and creek ecosystems. and heighten the experience of stone and water," said Snøhetta project director Matt McMahon.

The bridge was fabricated locally and is made of a stainless steel structure. It is primarily affixed to the north side of the gorge, where the bedrock is stronger, and cantilevers 46 feet (14 metres) to the other side.

The main structure was pre-fabricated and slotted into the slim site via crane.

The team then finished the bridge with black locust wood rails, concrete formed of rough-sawn hemlock, and a bluestone landing.

Read:

Moxon Architects adds "functional and graceful" bridge to Scottish highlands

Custom bronze castings of local flora and fauna such as an endangered dragonfly, a rare plant, and a model of the historic arch bridge were also distributed throughout the site for visitors to "pause and examine" the regional heritage of the area.

According to the team, the bridge frames views of the surrounding waterfalls and "heightens awareness of the mist and shifting light".

"The bridge demonstrates how thoughtful engineering can support both performance and experience," said Schlaich Bergermann Partner managing director Michael Stein.

"By developing a lightweight, cantilevered structure that could be prefabricated and installed with minimal impact on the gorge, we were able to create a resilient crossing that responds to the site's environmental sensitivities while enhancing the journey through one of New York’s most remarkable landscapes."

Other recently completed pedestrian bridges include a footbridge in France that spans over a 19th-century viaduct over the River Tarn and a low-lying bridge over a Belgian river.

item.content:encoded:
Agricultural barns and sheds informed the corrugated metal-clad volumes of House in a Clearing, a house in East Sussex completed by UK studio TaylorHare Architects.

When the clients purchased the site nestled in a woodland clearing near Uckfield, it was occupied by a small structure but already had planning permission for a much larger, two-storey dwelling.

The new owners, however, sought a quieter design that would feel more connected to the landscape, leading to TaylorHare Architects creating a cluster of three single-storey barns organised around a central courtyard informed by traditional farmsteads.

"Every design decision was measured against a simple question: did it strengthen the relationship between house and landscape?" director and project principal Christopher Taylor told Dezeen.

"Drawing on the character of rural agricultural steadings, the composition creates a home that feels both grounded and quietly expressive," he continued.

At the centre of House in a Clearing, a slightly larger building clad in black metal contains the main social spaces, which overlook both the paved courtyard and surrounding landscape through large windows.

A snug leads through into the bedroom wing, where a row of more intimate spaces sit off a long corridor and have also been given minimal, white finishes to emphasise external views through large openings framed in black metal.

To the south, a glazed link connects the living areas to an ancillary building, which contains a garage, home gym and guest room and is finished with a gable end of brickwork that the studio said "anchors the building in the landscape".

Read:

Charles Gillespie Architecture completes Somerset house with wildlife-friendly colonnade

All of the volumes are united by their finish of corrugated metal, which covers both their walls and roofs. According to the studio, this was chosen for its ability to make the home feel "both contemporary and deeply rooted in its setting".

The internal finishes of the home were kept purposefully minimal, with white walls and high gable ceilings complemented by pale oak timber in the bedrooms and stone paving in the kitchen and bathroom.

"White-rendered walls and natural timber create calm, light-filled spaces where the changing landscape, rather than the architecture itself, becomes the primary focus," Taylor told Dezeen.

"Ultimately, the materials were never intended to make a statement in their own right. Instead, they work together to create a building that feels enduring, familiar and quietly connected to its place."

Other recent homes in the UK that have taken cues from agricultural buildings include the transformation of a former tractor shed in Dorset into a low-carbon home by architecture practice Bindloss Dawes.

The photography is by Nick Dearden.
